title: Lip smacking and a pause
objective: Recognize subtle neonatal seizures (lip smacking, eye deviation, apnea), support EEG confirmation, look for treatable causes such as hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and infection, and expect phenobarbital as the first-line antiseizure drug

brief.situation: 09:30 in the NICU. You are the nurse for Baby Novak, a boy born at 37 weeks to a mother with diabetes, now 30 hours old. He has had three borderline glucose values and is on breast milk and formula feeds every 3 hours.
handover: His father says he 'did a funny chewing thing and stared to the side' for about half a minute, then 'held his breath' and went a little dusky.
Last glucose 4 hours ago was 47 mg/dL before a feed. He fed poorly at 09:00.

The neonatal nurse practitioner is on the unit. Unit protocol for a suspected seizure: protect the airway and support breathing, check a point-of-care glucose at once, send a serum glucose, calcium and electrolytes, and call the provider at once; IV dextrose and antiseizure drugs are given on the provider's order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: At 09:33 his eyes deviate to the left, he smacks his lips, his right arm 'cycles', and his breathing pauses for 15 seconds; saturation dips to 85% and recovers.
Axillary 36.6; no rash; fontanel soft and flat; no new risk in the chart for infection.
Three pre-feed glucose values in the 40s since birth; mother has insulin-treated diabetes.

why.question: What were Baby Novak's episodes, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Eye deviation, lip smacking, cycling and apnea are subtle neonatal seizures; in an infant of a diabetic mother with a glucose of 28, hypoglycemia is the likely treatable cause, with hypocalcemia and infection to rule out; EEG confirms.
parts.modelAnswer: Those are subtle seizures: the eye deviation, lip smacking, cycling and the apnea. He's an infant of a diabetic mother with a sugar of 28, so hypoglycemia is the likely cause, but calcium and infection need checking, and EEG confirms.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Protects the airway, checks glucose at once, sends glucose, calcium and electrolytes, calls the provider for IV dextrose and EEG; does not feed by mouth during spells.
parts.modelAnswer: Side-lying, clear the airway, oxygen during the spell, check his sugar now and send the labs, and call for IV dextrose and EEG. Nothing by mouth while he's seizing.

scoring.modelReasoning: Neonatal seizures are often subtle: chewing or lip smacking, eye deviation, cycling movements and apnea, and some are seen only on EEG. Treatable causes come first: hypoglycemia (likely here, an infant of a diabetic mother with a glucose of 28), hypocalcemia and infection, along with HIE and hemorrhage. Protect the airway, check glucose at once, send glucose, calcium and electrolytes, and call the provider for IV dextrose and EEG; antiseizure treatment is expected if seizures persist once the cause is corrected.
